title: Exploratory data analysis
bibliography: references.bib

```{r}
#| include: false

library(here)
library(gt)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(ggdist)
library(gghalves)

# Book plotting theme and legend helpers
Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")$value

# Read the cell data (one row per animal)
cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))

# Extreme values at day 7 (same injury, same survival time, very different response)
gfap_d7 <- cell_data$Gfap_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 7]
gfap_d7_range <- range(gfap_d7)
gfap_d7_fold <- gfap_d7_range[2] / gfap_d7_range[1]

# Day 30: find the widest gap between neighbouring animals (low group vs high group)
gfap_d30 <- sort(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 30])
gap_at <- which.max(diff(gfap_d30))
d30_low_max <- gfap_d30[gap_at]
d30_high_min <- gfap_d30[gap_at + 1]
d30_n_low <- gap_at
d30_n_high <- length(gfap_d30) - gap_at

# The one animal the usual boxplot rule flags at day 0
gfap_d0 <- cell_data[cell_data$DPI == 0, ]
d0_flag_value <- boxplot.stats(gfap_d0$Gfap_IntDen)$out
d0_flag_id <- gfap_d0$MouseID[gfap_d0$Gfap_IntDen %in% d0_flag_value]
d0_median <- median(gfap_d0$Gfap_IntDen)

# Numbers quoted in the text, computed from the data so they cannot drift
gfap_range <- range(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen)
gfap_mean_d0 <- mean(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 0])
gfap_mean_d7 <- mean(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 7])
gfap_sd_d0 <- sd(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 0])
gfap_sd_d7 <- sd(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 7])
r_pdgfrb_area <- cor(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen, cell_data$Tissue_Area)
r_area_dpi <- cor(cell_data$Tissue_Area, cell_data$DPI)
```

By now you've watched a posterior distribution get built, taken apart, and interrogated from every angle: priors, likelihood, MCMC, posterior predictive checks, the works. That machinery is honest, but it's also patient: it will just as happily process a badly-behaved dataset as a well-behaved one, and it won't warn you which kind you handed it. The one place where we already compared data against something, the `pp_check()` of @sec-mcmc-model-checking, was a look at the data *after* the model was fitted. This part is about the look that comes *before*, and about learning to do it ourselves instead of trusting a function to do it for us. Before we put the machinery to work on anything more ambitious than the `cell_data` comparison from @sec-intro-applied-modeling, I want to make sure you know how to look at your data: really look, not just glance at a mean and a standard deviation and move on.

## What is EDA?

Most of us know the temptation. The experiment is done, the lab meeting is on Thursday, and the fastest route to a slide is to feed the spreadsheet straight into a model or a test. Nobody would run a Western blot that way: you check the loading control before you trust the band. [Exploratory data analysis]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (EDA) is the same instinct applied to a spreadsheet instead of a gel. It means summarizing and visualizing your data before you model it, on purpose and systematically, looking for structure and patterns, and for the things that quietly break models: missing values, extreme values (outliers), and outright errors. Neuroscience data makes this more urgent than usual, because a single dataset can mix marker intensities, structural brain metrics, electrophysiological recordings, or cell counts from techniques like FACS, each with its own scale and its own ways of misbehaving.

The cornerstone of EDA is [visualization]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. In my own work, I trust a scatterplot faster than I trust a table of means and standard deviations; a plot shows me the shape of the data, while a summary table has already thrown that shape away and handed me two numbers instead. A scatterplot can reveal a nonlinear relationship that a correlation coefficient would flatten into a single misleading number; a boxplot can flag an extreme value that a mean would have quietly absorbed. @fig-eda-intro-shadow is the picture I keep in mind: a table of summaries is the shadow, and two quite different objects can cast the same one.

![Two very different objects, one identical shadow. A table of means and standard deviations is just the shadow; a plot is the object itself.](images/eda-intro_same-shadow-different-shape.png){#fig-eda-intro-shadow fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a small wooden table lit by a desk lamp, with a teal glass sphere and an upright ochre disc on it. On the wall behind, the two objects cast two identical round grey-blue shadows side by side."}

> EDA is not a formal process with a strict set of rules.
> More than anything, EDA is a state of mind.
> During the initial phases of EDA you should feel free to investigate every idea that occurs to you.
> Some of these ideas will pan out, and some will be dead ends.
> As your exploration continues, you will home in on a few particularly productive insights that you’ll eventually write up and communicate to others.
> [@wickham2023]

That state of mind has a practical consequence: EDA is a [dynamic and iterative process]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} of posing preliminary questions to your data and answering them with plots and basic summaries, not a checklist you tick once. It also has a limit worth stating now. What you spot while exploring is a lead, not a conclusion, and the plots that guide the model are not the evidence that confirms it.

::: callout-tip
A good analysis workflow begins with systematic and intentional EDA.
:::

## Performing exploratory data analysis

We'll practice on a dataset you've already met: `cell_data`, the glial scar study from @sec-intro-applied-modeling, with fluorescence measurements for PDGFR-β (a marker for pericytes) and GFAP (a marker for astrocytes and other astroglial lineage cells) across several days post-ischemia (DPI). A word on columns, because they will matter: the worked example in Part 1 used `Gfap_Intensity`, while this part mostly works with the integrated density columns `Gfap_IntDen` and `Pdgfrb_IntDen`, plus `Tissue_Area`, the area of the tissue section over which the cells were quantified. In @sec-intro-applied-modeling we asked one narrow question: sham-operated animals at day 0 against ischemic (MCAO) animals at day 3. Here we open the dataset back up and look at all of it, before asking anything more of it. The real code and figures come in @sec-eda-ggplot; this chapter is the map.

### First, what is a row?

The very first look needs no plot at all: what does one row represent, and which combinations of conditions actually exist? @tbl-eda-intro-design counts animals by condition and day.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-eda-intro-design
#| tbl-cap: Number of animals in `cell_data` by condition and day post-ischemia (DPI)

# Count animals for every combination of condition (rows) and day (columns)
as.data.frame.matrix(table(cell_data$Condition, cell_data$DPI)) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Condition") |>
  gt() |>
  tab_spanner(label = "DPI", columns = -Condition)
```

Two things stand out. Every row is one animal, and the design is lopsided: SHAM animals exist only at day 0, while MCAO animals are measured from day 3 to day 30.

::: callout-important
### A caveat on the Part 1 comparison

The comparison we made in @sec-intro-applied-modeling (SHAM at day 0 against MCAO at day 3) tangles the surgery with the passage of time: every SHAM animal we had was measured at day 0, so "SHAM vs. MCAO" and "day 0 vs. day 3" were, in that dataset, almost the same split. It was a fair first example for learning the mechanics of fitting a model, and the effect we found is real. But it is exactly the kind of fact that only shows up when you look at the design table instead of jumping straight to the model, and it will shape what questions this dataset can and cannot cleanly answer going forward.
:::

### Looking at distributions

Without first examining the data, we might [naively assume]{style="color:red;"} that fluorescence values follow a bell curve and proceed with methods built on that assumption. The assumption in a linear model is subtler than it sounds: it concerns the *residuals*, the variation left over once the predictors are accounted for (@sec-linear-regression-assumptions), not the raw column. Still, the raw distribution is where you start, and it often tells a different story from the one you expected. A [histogram or density plot]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} may reveal that the values are skewed, with a long tail, or that they pile up in two humps (@fig-eda-intro-fieldguide).

![Before you model, learn to recognize the species: the tidy hill, the two-humped camel, the long-tailed lizard. Each calls for a different kind of model.](images/eda-intro_field-guide-distributions.png){#fig-eda-intro-fieldguide fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of an open field notebook on a wooden bench showing three sketches whose outlines trace distribution curves: a symmetric hill with a small bird on top, a two-humped camel, and a long-tailed lizard with a steep back and a very long tail. Binoculars and a pencil rest beside the notebook."}

A two-humped shape is often a clue that you are looking at a mixture: two cell populations, or, as in `cell_data`, animals sampled at very different days lumped into one column. Pooled across days, `Gfap_IntDen` runs from about `r round(gfap_range[1])` to `r round(gfap_range[2])`, but the day-0 animals sit around `r round(gfap_mean_d0)` and the day-7 animals around `r round(gfap_mean_d7)`. A single histogram of the pooled values blends those groups, which is why the next move is always to ask whether the picture changes once you split it by the variables you know about.

### Looking at relationships

Beyond single variables, EDA examines how variables move together. A scatter plot of marker intensity against `Tissue_Area`, for example, shows a clear negative relationship (r ≈ `r sprintf("%.2f", r_pdgfrb_area)` for `Pdgfrb_IntDen`; @fig-eda-intro-gallery, panel A), and it is not hard to see why: the section shrinks as the injury progresses (r ≈ `r sprintf("%.2f", r_area_dpi)` between `Tissue_Area` and DPI) while the markers increase. Grouped boxplots, violin plots, or the raincloud plots we will build later (a half-density, the raw points, and a boxplot in one picture) show how location and [variability]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} change across groups or time points (panels B to D). That is where the second surprise of `cell_data` lives: the spread of `Gfap_IntDen` is not constant, with a standard deviation near `r round(gfap_sd_d0)` at day 0 against nearly `r round(gfap_sd_d7)` at day 7. These plots are not decorations for publication, adorned with asterisks and p-values. They are how we decide what to ask next.

Before we go deeper, I want you to see how much variety is on offer, because most of us were trained on one or two chart types (the bar of means with an asterisk on top, mostly). @fig-eda-intro-gallery is a first taste, and nothing more: the real code, and the reasoning behind each choice, come in @sec-eda-ggplot. Panels B, C and D draw the very same `r nrow(cell_data)` animals three ways, so you can watch each chart type reveal, or hide, something different.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eda-intro-gallery
#| fig-cap: "Four ways of looking at `cell_data`. A: scatter plot of PDGFR-β against tissue area, one point per animal. B to D: GFAP integrated density by day post-ischemia drawn as a boxplot (B), a violin plot (C) and a raincloud plot (D)."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels. A: scatter plot in which ischemic animals, drawn as blue triangles, show higher PDGFR-β integrated density at smaller tissue areas, while sham animals, drawn as orange circles, sit at large tissue area and low PDGFR-β. B: boxplots of GFAP integrated density rising from day 0 to day 7 and staying high through day 30, with a much wider box at day 7. C: violin plots of the same data; day 30 narrows in the middle, hinting at two humps. D: raincloud plots combining half-densities, boxplots and individual animals for each day."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

# Colorblind-safe colours (Okabe-Ito); the scatter also uses shape, so it reads in grayscale
okabe_ito <- c(SHAM = "#E69F00", MCAO = "#0072B2")

# Day as a category, so each day gets its own box, violin or cloud
cell_data$DPI_f <- factor(cell_data$DPI)

# Smaller text than the single-figure theme, so four panels fit on one page
Plot_theme_small <- Plot_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 11),
    axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.8),
    axis.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 0.6),
    axis.ticks.length = unit(4, "pt")
  )

# A: one point per animal; the legend sits in the empty upper right corner
p_scatter <- ggplot(cell_data, aes(Tissue_Area, Pdgfrb_IntDen,
                                   color = Condition, shape = Condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(SHAM = 16, MCAO = 17)) +
  labs(title = "Scatter plot", x = "Tissue area (mm²)",
       y = "PDGFR-β integrated density") +
  Plot_theme_small + legend_inside(0.82, 0.85)

# B: five-number summary per day
p_box <- ggplot(cell_data, aes(DPI_f, Gfap_IntDen)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.6, width = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Boxplot", x = "Days post-ischemia", y = "GFAP integrated density") +
  Plot_theme_small

# C: the whole shape of the distribution per day
p_violin <- ggplot(cell_data, aes(DPI_f, Gfap_IntDen)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.55, width = 0.9, scale = "width") +
  labs(title = "Violin plot", x = "Days post-ischemia", y = "GFAP integrated density") +
  Plot_theme_small

# D: half-density (the cloud), boxplot, and every animal (the rain)
p_rain <- ggplot(cell_data, aes(DPI_f, Gfap_IntDen)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.6, width = 0.6, .width = 0, normalize = "groups",
               justification = -0.2, point_colour = NA,
               fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_half_point(side = "l", range_scale = 0.35, alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) +
  labs(title = "Raincloud plot", x = "Days post-ischemia", y = "GFAP integrated density") +
  Plot_theme_small

# Assemble the four panels and tag them A to D
(p_scatter | p_box) / (p_violin | p_rain) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

A word on why the figure looks like this, since it is not the default most of us inherited. Everything is drawn with `ggplot2` [@wickham2016], the clouds with `ggdist::stat_halfeye()` [@ggdist] and the raw points with `gghalves::geom_half_point()` [@gghalves], and the panels are stitched together with `patchwork` [@patchwork]. The reason to prefer these forms is that each day here holds only `r min(table(cell_data$DPI))` to `r max(table(cell_data$DPI))` animals. A bar of means with an asterisk would squeeze each of those groups into one number and one star, and you would never learn that the spread explodes after day 3. A design tip you can steal for your own figures: when the groups are small, show every animal.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this gallery"}
Start with panel A: each point is one animal, its position says how large its section was and how much PDGFR-β it showed, and the shape and color tell you whether it was sham or ischemic. Now compare panels B, C and D, which share the same y-axis. In the boxplot, the box holds the middle half of the animals and the thick line is the median. In the violin, width means "many animals have values around here". In the raincloud, you get the width *and* the animals themselves, so you can count them. What to look for is the spread: the day 0 box is tiny and the day 7 box is enormous, and each chart tells you so in its own way. The one mistake to avoid is reading a smooth violin as if it held thousands of observations; each one here rests on about ten animals.
:::

Two ideas often get mixed up at this stage, and they deserve their own names. Two predictors that are strongly correlated with each other (like `Pdgfrb_Area` and `Pdgfrb_IntDen`) are [collinear]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: they carry overlapping information, and a model that includes both will struggle to apportion credit between them (two thermometers taped side by side tell you the temperature, but not which of them to thank). A [confounder]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} is something different: a variable that influences both the predictor you care about and the outcome, and so can manufacture or hide an association (if the sham mice were all stained in Monday's batch and the ischemic ones on Thursday's, the batch is a confounder of the group difference you think you see). Here, DPI plays that role in the relationship between the two markers. Plots can alert you to both, but only your knowledge of the experiment tells you which one you are looking at. We screen for collinearity systematically in @sec-eda-ggpairs and quantify it on a fitted model in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions.

### Looking for extreme values

Finally, EDA is how you find the points that sit far from the rest of the data. The usual name for them is [outliers]{.ix ix="extreme values"}, and I am going to avoid the word as much as I can, because it arrives with a verdict attached. An outlier is something that lies *outside*: a stray, a nuisance, a row to be tidied away so that the real analysis can begin. A plot cannot tell you any of that. All it can tell you is that a point is far from the others, so I prefer to call these [extreme values]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, and to treat the name as a description, not a diagnosis.

Here is why I care. Behind every extreme value in our data there is a mouse. Take the animals in `cell_data` at day 7 after ischemia: same surgery, same survival time, processed and imaged by the same hands. Their GFAP integrated density runs from `r round(gfap_d7_range[1])` to `r round(gfap_d7_range[2])`, a `r round(gfap_d7_fold)`-fold range. The animal at the bottom barely reacted; the one at the top reacted fiercely. Nobody made a mistake. That is what biology does when you hand it the same injury more than once, and plausible reasons are easy to list (the size of the infarct, how much collateral blood flow each animal had, how strong its inflammatory response was). At day 30 the picture is sharper still: `r d30_n_low` animals sit at or below `r round(d30_low_max)`, `r d30_n_high` sit at or above `r round(d30_high_min)`, and not one lies in between. If I had called the low ones outliers and deleted them, I would not have cleaned my data. I would have erased the mice that did not respond, and my paper would have described a response that every animal had, which is not the response nature gave me.

The same logic holds for a treatment. Some animals do not respond to it at all, others respond dramatically, and that is a finding in itself (who responds, and why?), not noise around the finding. A mean computed after trimming the extremes is a story about an average mouse that does not exist, told with an interval too narrow to be honest about it.

None of this means an extreme value is always real. Extreme values can be errors: a stain that failed, a mislabeled tube, a section cut at the wrong level. In `cell_data`, the usual boxplot rule flags exactly one animal, `r d0_flag_id`, a sham mouse at day 0 with a GFAP integrated density of `r round(d0_flag_value)` against a median of `r round(d0_median)` for its group. From the table alone, I cannot tell whether that is a stain that did not take or a mouse with a very quiet baseline. The lab notebook and the microscope session can. So the habit I try to keep is to *ask first, write down the answer, and delete only for a reason that has nothing to do with the number being inconvenient*. It matters, because a single extreme point can dominate a fit and produce a "significant" result that disappears without it, and because removing a point for being inconvenient is its own kind of bias. When an extreme value is legitimate, the better answer is usually a model that expects it, such as the Student-t regression in @sec-beta-robust-regression, and when you are genuinely unsure, report the analysis with and without it.

::: callout-tip
### Exploratory data analysis in action

What a few minutes of looking already told us about `cell_data`:

-   **The design has a shape:** [A table of counts]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} showed that SHAM animals exist only at day 0, so surgery and time cannot be separated for them.
-   **The spread is not constant:** [A grouped plot]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} would show `Gfap_IntDen` varying far more at day 7 than at day 0, a warning for any model that assumes one common variance.
-   **Variables overlap and move together:** [A scatter plot]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} of `Pdgfrb_IntDen` against `Tissue_Area` shows a strong negative association that is mostly riding on DPI, the kind of overlap that can bias a model if used carelessly.
-   **Extreme values deserve a question, not an eraser:** [A raincloud plot]{style="text-decoration: underline;"} shows that animals given the same injury can differ `r round(gfap_d7_fold)`-fold in GFAP at day 7. That spread is biology to model, and it only becomes an error once the lab notebook says so.
:::

## Take home message

EDA is not a preliminary or optional step; it is how you learn what your data can and cannot support before a model starts making claims for you. By exploring systematically, we identify trends, patterns, and anomalies, and we make explicit the assumptions that will guide what comes next. It also makes our work reproducible, but only if the exploration lives in a script rather than in a session that closes and is forgotten (see @sec-appendix-open-science).

Here's the plan for the rest of this part. First, @sec-eda-first-look takes the quickest look there is: a table, before any plot, which already turns up a missing value, two misspelled column names and a duplicated unit. @sec-eda-data-quality then fixes the names and the duplicate properly, in a script rather than by hand in the spreadsheet, and adds validation rules that stop the analysis when a value breaks them; the raw CSV stays untouched. @sec-eda-missing-data comes back for that one missing value, finds that it left a wrong-looking-fine number in a derived column, and asks what it can and cannot tell us. Only then do we turn to @sec-eda-ggplot, working through `cell_data` in detail with `ggplot2`: the density plots, scatter plots, and raincloud plots this chapter has been previewing. After that, @sec-eda-gwalkr lets you drive, exploring the same dataset freely and interactively with GwalkR. Then @sec-eda-ggpairs zooms out from single variables to the relationships between all of them at once, screening for redundant predictors before they can bite us later. We close the part with @sec-eda-summary, pulling everything we've found into one place: the running list of things we now know about `cell_data` that will shape every modeling decision from here on.
